meta.name: Jay BIPU Content Idea Tournament — History Round
meta.pain_first_rule: An idea can only win by demonstrating the reader's pain more precisely than its opponent. Solution quality scores nothing until pain recognition scores.
meta.provenance: Ideas synthesized from recent project themes in agent history and the Jay Yang copywriting essay. Raw private transcripts, credentials, and identifiers are not included.

pods.name: Receipt Debt
pods.theme: The work is real, but the claim has no inspectable artifact behind it
ideas: Your thesis is not weak because people disagree with it; it is weak because the artifact that could let them check it does not exist yet.
A green status page is not proof of a working system. The receipt is the system's first honest sentence.
You keep polishing the claim because publishing the failed test would reveal whether there was ever a test underneath it.
The gap between what your README promises and what a stranger can run is where trust goes to die.

pods.name: The Complexity Tax
pods.theme: The system feels costly to understand, but the cost has not been isolated or measured
ideas: You are calling it burnout because 'too many dependent states with no reset boundary' sounds less sympathetic and more expensive to investigate.
The hidden cost of a complex system is not that it has more parts; it is that one missing state can make every later decision look rational and still be wrong.
If complexity is real, changing the number of dependencies should change the receipt. Otherwise you have a metaphor, not a measurement.
The body keeps paying for information you never compressed because nobody can point to which state is safe to forget.

pods.name: The Autonomy Mirage
pods.theme: The agent appears capable until boundaries, permissions, and readback are tested
ideas: An agent that can click everything is not autonomous; it is unsupervised. Autonomy starts where the forbidden action is legible.
You do not need an agent that promises to handle the world. You need one that can say exactly what it touched and what it refused.
The demo is not the agent completing the happy path. The demo is the agent stopping at the boundary and leaving a receipt you can inspect.
If the agent's history cannot tell you why it acted, the system is not learning from work; it is accumulating anecdotes.

pods.name: Attribution Blindness
pods.theme: Attention, clicks, and payments arrive without enough provenance to know what caused them
ideas: Traffic is not traction when you cannot tell which sentence moved the person or which path brought them there.
The sale did not disappear; your attribution disappeared first, and now every explanation is a story with a confidence interval you refuse to show.
A dashboard full of visits can still leave you blind if it cannot answer which pain the visitor recognized before they acted.
If your funnel records the conversion but not the path, you are measuring the ending and guessing at the mechanism.

pods.name: The Edge-Case Bill
pods.theme: The happy path works while operational failures accumulate outside the demo
ideas: Your system did not fail suddenly; it failed in the one branch the demo never had to visit.
A deployment is not finished when the homepage returns 200. It is finished when the provider rejects a request and the user gets an honest next step.
The bug is rarely the dramatic outage. It is the silent mismatch between the account, the domain, the webhook, and the thing you thought you configured.
Every untested edge case is a future support conversation you are pre-paying with someone else's trust.

pods.name: The Incomplete-Information Trap
pods.theme: The reader waits for certainty while the useful next experiment remains undone
ideas: You are not waiting for more information; you are waiting for information that removes the risk of being visibly wrong.
A bounded experiment can teach you more than another week of research, but only if you decide what result would make you stop.
The cost of waiting is not time in the abstract. It is the evidence you could have collected before the next decision became expensive.
Start messy is not permission to improvise forever; it is a demand to ship the smallest falsifier before the story hardens.

judge_archetypes.name: The Skimmer
judge_archetypes.note: 3-second scroll test: only the first line and the felt punch register.

judge_archetypes.name: The Busy Operator
judge_archetypes.note: $1-3M owner skimming between meetings: does this name MY Tuesday afternoon?

judge_archetypes.name: The Skeptical Buyer
judge_archetypes.note: Wants receipts. Attacks unsupported claims. Rewards pointable evidence.

judge_archetypes.name: The Pattern Hunter
judge_archetypes.note: Rewards the Everyone-thinks-X / Problem-is-Y / Solution-is-Z structure.

judge_archetypes.name: The Tired Scroller
judge_archetypes.note: Reading at 3rd-grade level after a long day: anything requiring work is a loss.

format.round1: Within each pod, ideas face off pairwise; winners advance.
format.final: Pod champions meet in cross-pod round-robin judged by all archetypes.
format.scoring: Each judge returns pain_recognition (0-5), specificity (0-5), action_pull (0-3). Pain recognition is weighted double and gates: if tied or losing on pain recognition, an idea cannot win regardless of other axes.
format.tiebreak: Higher pain_recognition, then higher specificity, then earlier seed order.
